I grew up in the NE United States.  I never like to say "east coast" cause I did not grow up on the coast.
Growing up, my family got pizza from a place called "joes".  It's not the best pizza I have ever had, but it was great and I ate it a lot growing up.  I have fond memories of that pie.

When Pok Pok opened, a wave of nostalgia washed over my pallet.  The food there took me back to my childhood.  It reminded me of the food I had (and hadn't eaten since) at the homes of Laotian friends houses growing up.

Red Sauce pizza has had a similar effect on my pallet.  It reminds me of Joe's Pizza.  It's the most joyful pizza I have eaten in Portland.
Pizza Jerk on the other hand, reminds me of Bunk sandwiches.  Good sandwiches that work as motivation for the gym, while Red Sauce is pure nostalgia that works as motivation for red wine.

Alaska weddings are the best! Especially when they take place outside and then the reception is a potluck at a place like the dog mushers' hall in Fairbanks. Kids and dogs running around everywhere, salmon, beer and the music provided by the bride and groom, and everyone bringing food to share at the celebration. Emily Post would roll over in her grave, but I'll take this kind of wedding over a fancy, over-priced one any day.
We had a nice ceremony in Hatcher's Pass and a reception/BBQ at home.  Spent the money on a Belize honeymoon.  Way better than spending thousands for flowers, cake, and a reception hall.

Wife and me got married in Fairbanks in '76. Her sister made the cake and reception was a cookout with friends and family. For around $100.00 we were surrounded by real friends and family with an Alaskan relaxation and no debt. I married one of my sons, a friend married another of my son's and yet another one was married in the wife's yard at one of the best weddings ever. Again no debt, just good ole fashion Alaskan scenary, barbecues and fun.

Small family restaurants are becoming fewer and fewer due to large increases in rent and the high cost of labour.  Those costs are passed on to customers. 10 dollar Caesar salad anyone? Four restaurants in my area that have been here for decades closed down for those reasons. One place in particular had its rent doubled by new property owners forcing them to close down after a few months.  Big chains like Cactus Club, White Spot and Earl's are better able to withstand this sort of thing so they attract better talent while keeping prices affordable.

replies.text: Actually the number of restaurants in the central area of Vancouver has increased significantly. It would help if you precisely defined 'family' restaurant. If you mean by that a smaller restaurant with 20' - 30' of frontage that's not part of the chain, then the additional restaurants in the central area are 'family' restaurants. Also in there will always be a lot of churn in restaurants - many do not survive more than a year or two. In this area, the majority of the population are 20 -40 years old and there is a significant number of babies being born and a school being built on Expo because the schools are full. It's a different world and yes the larger chain restaurants are a significant part of the scene. You will also find couples with young children in restaurants even in Gastown and in the larger restaurants like the Cactus Club.

I agree that operating restaurants are a risky affair at best. What I mean by family restaurants are businesses who are family run. I suspect the reality of running a restaurant in Gastown or in Kits is different than operating one in, let's say, White Rock or Langley. There is a significant number of families in the 'burbs but perhaps they are less able to afford to the aforementioned 10 dollar Caesar salad. Restaurants in the burbs probably get far less traffic than downtown unless you are in a mall where chains are often already established. In Hungarian, the word for tomato is the same as the word for paradise.  Tomatoes are a huge part of Hungarian cuisine, and I can just imagine the first time that a Hungarian bit into a tomato some 500 years ago and was blown away.  But that's hardly the case anymore (though you might still get lucky in Hungary and places like Italy and have a tomato that reminds you of what they were like decades ago here in Canada).

Right now, I'm about to go out grocery shopping, and am looking for apples.  There's another fruit that could use an upgrade. Beautiful big shiny red or yellow tomatoes abound in our grocery stores.  But when you bite into most of them, you may as well be eating plastic.  Big and beautiful do not a good taste necessarily make.

Kitchen talk.text: Really! Let them eat cake!!

And another reason:

Bringing your own birthday cake is not just an issue for the restaurant.  Consider that your guests and, particularly your guest of honour, may be deeply insulted that you cheaped out on a tawdry and tasteless grocery store cake.  In my experience, most people (even sugar-sucking kids) don’t finish the cake on their plate and somehow manage to politely decline the offer of seconds.  And no one, I mean NO ONE, ever agrees to take home the remaining cake (of which, not surprisingly, there is often quite a lot).

And another reason:

There is really no return on your investment.  Grocery store cakes range between about $8 and $28, depending upon their size and, for lack of a better word, “intricacy”.  If, in addition, the restaurant charges a plating fee, then the cost of your store-bought cake will likely exceed the cost of having the restaurant make a cake for you in the first place.  A restaurant might charge between $30 and $50 for a cake, depending upon the size and type, and I guarantee your guests will fight over the leftovers, if there are any.

For years we have  been celebrating birthday dinners at favourite restaurants.  They are all upscale and happy to have us there spending a VERY large amount of money.  We have a famous family recipe that is birthday tradition and my kids - now grown - feel that it is not a birthday without it.  You can't compare bringing a roast chicken with bringing a birthday cake.  The restaurants we go to have never made a fuss and in fact seem quite happy to see a family enjoying this tradition in their restaurant, although now I wonder if they're all in the kitchen swearing at us.   If restaurants are going to be insulted over something that has nothing to do with their skill then yes - maybe we should stay home and spend our $1000 on something else,  or we will go home for dessert.   I am a gracious generous customer with enormous respect everyone - those who bus to the genius chefs in the kitchen - but a birthday is a special celebration of sentiment and love.  A cake is a gift of that love.
I like to make a special cake for my husband's birthday, but we like to go out for a nice meal. Then we go home and have the cake. That generally results in two desserts. What's not to like?
Reminds me of my days working in restaurants.....people would order a cup or pot of hot water, then shamelessly pull out their used tea bags.
Is this what Canadians do?  I've eaten out a fair bit in the US and I've only seen cakes brought into restaurants that really don't do traditional cake desserts (like Chinese restaurants).

The point of gong to a restaurant is to make the event special. It might be due lack of space elsewhere or the ability to cook for that many people.

Some places have rules about reservations, seating, food, alcohol etc...I understand that they are not in control of some of these requirements. And, has been suggested elsewhere, not every eatery is equipped to provide a special dessert or cake for the event.

In all of this, if they can't or won't accommodate such a request, then this will likely be remembered by the group the next time they have another event to plan. They may even speak with others who might voice similar ideas.

Yeah, the restaurant may get their way short term.

Long term, they may live to regret such rigid thinking.

I often try new recipes and test them on my very willing husband. but when I host, I serve what I know my guests will enjoy in order to maximize their enjoyment of the evening since enjoyment is the goal. If these coffee shop owners really want to 'pull the plug' and create a more social experience, they need to have an explicit no phone or laptop policy.  I know of a tea house that does just that.

These 'unplugged' coffee shops will then need to provide alternative things to do that encourage socializing.  Maybe board games? And they need to create an interesting and welcoming atmosphere with their interior design, music, seating, outdoor patio, etc.   But above all, they need to learn how to make killer coffee.  They can get away with so-so coffee if people are there just to use the WiFi.  But if you want people to actually go for the coffee, and maybe to socialize, then you will actually need to make good coffee.
That said, if the people in the neighbourhood are not really interested in these things - and just want WiFi - then it will be hard to be successful.  Ultimately, coffee shops are a reflection of the local people.

I've had mine for about two years.  It's amazing.  I just completed a six week long, complete kitchen reno in my Ottawa home, and the Instant Pot saved me.  No ordering in take-out food every night! I did buy a roast chicken from a grocery chain store one night, but threw the bones into the instant pot and made broth under two hours, which I used for my risotto the next night (making it under an hour), and not requiring constant stirring like I would if made it on the stove-top.

While us baby boomers may have grown up with a pressure cooker in the kitchen, they always scared the living bejesus out of me. An amazing thing about the Instant Pot is how quiet it is while under pressure. We find it great for everyday meals like stews and soups - the flavours are intense and the meal is ready in minutes instead of hours.
